statement: A list starts with 49. Each new number is the sum of the digits of the number before it, plus 5. So the list begins 49, 18, 14, 10, ... What is the 100th number in the list?

choices.misconception: I gave the 99th number instead of the 100th.
I let the repeating block 14, 10, 6, 11, 7, 12, 8, 13, 9 start at the second number instead of the third.
I let the repeating block 14, 10, 6, 11, 7, 12, 8, 13, 9 start at the first number instead of the third.
I put 49 and 18 into the repeating block, using a block of eleven numbers, but 49 and 18 never come back.

hints: Write out the first twelve or so numbers and watch for a repeat.
Once a number comes back, the list repeats from there forever. Find where the repeating block starts and how long it is, then work out where the 100th number falls in the block.
The list is 49, 18, 14, 10, 6, 11, 7, 12, 8, 13, 9, 14, ... From the 3rd number on, the block 14, 10, 6, 11, 7, 12, 8, 13, 9 repeats. The 100th number is the 98th number of this repeating part.

solutions.reliable: Following the rule: 49, 18, 14, 10, 6, 11, 7, 12, 8, 13, 9, 14, ... After 9 comes 9 + 5 = 14 again, so from the 3rd number onwards the block 14, 10, 6, 11, 7, 12, 8, 13, 9 of length 9 repeats, and 49 and 18 never return. The 100th number is number 98 of the repeating part. Since 98 = 10 × 9 + 8, it is the 8th number of the block, which is 13. The transferable idea: when a rule makes a list repeat, find where the cycle starts and how long it is, then use remainders.

whyOnTest: Recursive rules often fall into a cycle. Spotting it, and noticing that the first two numbers are outside it, is the 4-point skill.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
